names.name: Nimbu mirchi
names.th: นิมบู มีร์ชี (มะนาวกับพริก)

etymology.root: Hindi nīmbū 'lime, lemon' + mirchī 'chilli' — the object is named by its two ingredients and nothing else
etymology.note: The wider class word is nazar battu, from nazar, the harmful look, in Hindustani.

text.what: A lime and seven green chillies threaded on a string and hung at a doorstep, over a shop counter or from the back of a vehicle. Nothing is worn and nothing is written. The thing rots in the sun, browns, and is replaced.
text.story:
Two explanations of the same string circulate, and they disagree about who the string is for.

In Hindu households, especially in northern India, hanging a lime and seven green chillies at the doorstep is a ritual to either ward off or acknowledge Alakshmi, the goddess of misfortune and grief, whose name means not-Lakshmi. One version holds that the sourness of the lime and the pungency of the chillies together make a smell even Alakshmi cannot tolerate. The other holds that Alakshmi is pleased by sour and spicy offerings, and will take her share standing at the door — which makes the string a payment at the threshold rather than a barrier across it. Alakshmi is not named in Vedic, Upanishadic or early Puranic literature; she is named in the Linga Purana, the Padma Purana and the Śrī Sūkta.

The string also belongs to a wider North Indian and Pakistani class, the nazar battu, whose logic is spoilage. A nazar battu is often a deliberate blemish introduced to prevent perfection: a black mark on the face or neck of a loved one, a flaw built into an otherwise faultless house, a stitching or colouring error put into an expensive carpet or sari. Mothers lightly spit to the side of their children to imply disparagement, and children are marked with a black spot on the cheek, because excessive admiration — even from well-meaning people, even a mother's own love — is held to draw nazar.

*Inference —* a lime and chillies at a shop door belong to that logic rather than to the eye-against-the-eye logic of the Mediterranean. The object is not looking back. It is either an imperfection hung where the perfect thing is, or a plate left out for the guest nobody wants inside.
text.how: Bought made up, at the price of a lime. Threaded so the chillies hang below the fruit, tied at a lintel, a counter, a bumper or a dashboard. It is a household act, not a specialist's: no source read here names a priest, a mantra or a consecration for it.
text.today: Ordinary street furniture in North Indian and Pakistani towns as of 2026, on shopfronts, new cars and trucks. The phrase nazar battu has also gone idiomatic: commentators in North India and Pakistan use it for a person or thing that is unwanted but has to be tolerated, as some of the press did of Pervez Musharraf during Pakistan's transition to democracy at the 2008 general election.

dating.period: not dated in the sources read
dating.label: undated; carried now
dating.note: The texts that name Alakshmi — the Linga Purana, the Padma Purana, the Śrī Sūkta — are not dated in the source, and the source dates the doorstep practice not at all. A start year would be invented, so there is none.

object.made_by: anybody; sold ready-strung at markets and traffic lights
object.note: The count of seven green chillies with one lime is the one given in the source. Replacement when it dries is the ordinary practice; no source read here states an interval, so none is given.
